content: 1. Lymphatic filariasis is caused by parasitic nematodes such as Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, and Brugia timori. 2. Cutaneous filariasis is caused by Onchocerca volvulus and Loa loa. 3. Onchocerciasis, also known as river blindness, is treated with ivermectin. The preferred regimen is a single dose of 150 mcg/kg orally, repeated every 6–12 months until the patient becomes asymptomatic. 4. If ivermectin fails, an alternative treatment is suramin. 5. When both Onchocerca and Loa loa infections are present, a peripheral smear should be performed. If Loa loa microfilariae are detected, treat Onchocerca first with ivermectin before using diethylcarbamazine (DEC) for Loa loa. 6. Retreatment for microfilaremia is often necessary every 6–12 months, as demonstrated by repeat blood smear or antigen testing. 7. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) should not be used in Onchocerca volvulus infections due to the increased risk of precipitating blindness. 8. Treating the endosymbiont Wolbachia bacteria may help clear the infection. The preferred regimen is doxycycline 100 mg once or twice daily for 6–8 weeks. This treatment is particularly effective for co-infecting pathogens such as Wuchereria or Onchocerca, but its effect on Loa loa is less significant. 9. For Loa loa cutaneous filariasis (eye worm disease), the preferred treatment is diethylcarbamazine (DEC) with a gradual dose escalation to reduce adverse reactions. The regimen includes: Day 1: 50 mg Day 2: 50 mg three times daily Day 3: 100 mg three times daily Days 4–21: 8–10 mg/kg/day in three divided doses. 10. An alternative treatment for Loa loa is albendazole 200 mg orally twice daily for 21 days. 11. If Loa loa microfilariae exceed 5,000/mL of blood, DEC can cause encephalopathy. In such cases, albendazole may be initiated for a few days, with or without steroids, before starting DEC. 12. For Wuchereria bancrofti lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis), the preferred treatment is a scaled dose of DEC with gradual escalation to reduce reactions: Day 1: 50 mg Day 2: 50 mg three times daily Day 3: 100 mg three times daily Days 4–14: 2 mg/kg every 8 hours for a total of 72 mg over 14 days. 13. Corticosteroids or antihistamines may be required to manage allergic reactions caused by dying microfilariae. 14. For Brugia malayi and Brugia timori lymphatic filariasis, the treatment regimen is similar to that for Wuchereria bancrofti. 15. Skin snips can be used to detect Onchocerca volvulus or Mansonella streptocerca. 16. For Echinococcus multilocularis (alveolar cyst disease), the preferred treatment is albendazole. For patients weighing ≥60 kg, the dose is 400 mg orally twice daily with meals. For patients weighing <60 kg, the dose is 15 mg/kg/day divided into two doses. 17. Neurocysticercosis (NCC), caused by the larval form of Taenia solium, is treated as follows: For intestinal tapeworms, praziquantel 5–10 mg/kg orally as a single dose is recommended. For parenchymal NCC, albendazole is preferred. For patients weighing ≥60 kg, the dose is 400 mg twice daily with meals. For patients weighing <60 kg, the dose is 15 mg/kg/day in two divided doses (maximum 1 g/day). Treatment duration is 8–30 days, with or without anti-seizure medication. An alternative regimen for parenchymal NCC is praziquantel 100 mg/kg/day in three divided doses for 29 days. For degenerating cysts, the same albendazole regimen is used as for parenchymal NCC. For subarachnoid NCC, albendazole is combined with shunting for hydrocephalus. 18. For myiasis (fly larvae infestation), the preferred treatment involves occluding the punctum to prevent gas exchange using petroleum jelly, nail polish, makeup cream, or bacon. When the larvae migrate, they can be manually removed. 19. For pubic lice (Pthirus pubis), the treatment involves applying 5% permethrin lotion to dry hair for 8–12 hours, followed by shampooing. Two doses are given 7–9 days apart. An alternative is ivermectin 200 mcg/kg orally as a single dose, with three doses at 7-day intervals reported to be effective. 20. For scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei), the treatment depends on the patient’s immune status: In immunocompetent patients, the preferred treatment is permethrin 5% cream (Elimite). An alternative is ivermectin 200 mcg/kg orally as a single dose, with a second dose if symptoms persist. Another less effective option is crotamiton 10% cream, applied for 24 hours, rinsed off, and reapplied for another 24 hours. In immunocompromised patients, such as those with AIDS (CD4 <150/mm³), ivermectin 200 mcg/kg orally is effective, but multiple doses separated by 14 days may be required. 21. For adenovirus infections, treatment includes administering 1.25 g/m² of probenecid three hours before cidofovir infusion and three and nine hours after each infusion. Alternatively, cidofovir 1 mg/kg IV can be given three times per week. 22. For hemorrhagic cystitis caused by adenovirus, supportive care is recommended. 23. For bronchitis, refer to the Johns Hopkins ABX Guide for diagnosis and treatment recommendations.
